summary: This note covers late Roman religious conflict and change. It describes the Diocletianic persecution of Christians beginning around 302-303, including edicts ordering church destruction and mandating sacrifice, and the executions of Maximilian and Marcellus, who refused military service. It then notes how Roman military settlement spread varied cults, and how Julian's brief revival attempt was followed by Theodosius I making Nicene Christianity the state religion in 380, while many pre-Christian practices survived within Christianity.
one_line: Overview of late Roman religious policy, from the Diocletianic persecution of Christians to Nicene Christianity becoming the Roman state religion under Theodosius I.
key_facts: In 295, a certain Maximilian refused military service and was executed for treason; he was a Christian.
In 298, Marcellus renounced his military oath and was executed for treason; he was a Christian.
Around 302, a report of ominous haruspicy in Diocletian's domus, followed by an undated dictat of placatory sacrifice by the entire military, triggered a series of edicts against Christianity.
The first edict (303 AD) ordered the destruction of church buildings and Christian texts and forbade services to be held.
The first edict degraded officials who were Christians, re-enslaved imperial freedmen who were Christians, and reduced the legal rights of all Christians.
Under the first edict, physical or capital punishments were not imposed on Christians, but soon after, several Christians suspected of attempted arson in the palace were executed.
The second edict threatened Christian priests with imprisonment.
The third edict offered Christians freedom if they performed sacrifice.
An edict of 304 enjoined universal sacrifice to traditional gods, in terms that recall the Decian edict.
Roman citizen-soldiers set up altars to multiple deities, including traditional gods, the Imperial genius and local deities.
Roman citizen-soldiers sometimes used the dedication diis deabusque omnibus (all the gods and goddesses).
The later granting of citizenship to provincials and their conscription into the legions brought their new cults into the Roman military.
The emperor Julian made a short-lived attempt to revive traditional and Hellenistic religion and to affirm the special status of Judaism.
In 380, under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became the official state religion of the Roman Empire.
Pleas for religious tolerance from the senator Symmachus (d. 402) were rejected.
Heretics as well as non-Christians were subject to exclusion from public life or persecution after Christianity became dominant.
Many pre-Christian beliefs and practices survived in Christian festivals and local traditions.
